Input real numbers $a<b$, an integer $n\ge2$, and a real-valued function
$f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ evaluable at every point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the
procedure returns invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. If $a\ge b$ or
$n<2$, the procedure returns invalid-grid. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.
hypotheses: The level hierarchy explicitly sets Q_l=Q_S(.;0,1,2^(l+1)); matched inputs are a<b, an even panel count at least two, and the exact-real finite weighted-sum convention.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^4([a,b])$, set $M_4=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(4)}(x)|$. Then the value
$Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_S(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180}M_4.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.

Let $a<b$, $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, and $f\in C[a,b]$. For $n\ge1$, set $g(t):=f(m+dt)$ on $[-1,1]$, let $y_j=g(\cos(j\pi/n))$, and form $a_0,\ldots,a_n$ from the DCT-I coefficients in [[thm-na-clenshaw-curtis-interpolation-coefficients]]. With the Chebyshev moments $\mu_k$ of [[lem-na-chebyshev-integral-moments]], define
$$Q_{n,[a,b]}(f):=d\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k\mu_k.$$
For $n=0$, define instead
$$Q_{0,[a,b]}(f):=(b-a)f(m),$$
the midpoint rule. This is the explicit endpoint and zero-degree convention for Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature. The sums and coefficients are exact real quantities; finite-precision evaluation is a separate algorithm.

excerpt:
Let $a<b$, $n\ge0$, and $f\in C[a,b]$. Put $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, and $g(t)=f(m+dt)$ on $[-1,1]$. Let $E_n(g)$ and $\Lambda_n^L$ be the best uniform polynomial error and the Chebyshev–Lobatto interpolation norm from [[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]]. The rule $Q_{n,[a,b]}$ of [[def-na-clenshaw-curtis-quadrature]] is exact for every polynomial of degree at most $n$, and
$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_{n,[a,b]}(f)\right|\le(b-a)(1+\Lambda_n^L)E_n(g).$$
Because affine pullback preserves the supremum norm and polynomial degree, $E_n(g)$ is also the best degree-$n$ uniform error of $f$ on $[a,b]$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

excerpt:
Let $d\ge1$ and, for each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$Q_j(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}w_i^{(j)}f(x_i^{(j)})$ be a well-defined Gaussian rule
as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]] and
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]]. Its **tensor-product
quadrature rule** is
$$ Q_{\otimes}(f):= \sum_{i_1=1}^{m_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{m_d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}w_{i_j}^{(j)}\right) f\left(x_{i_1}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{i_d}^{(d)}\right). $$
Its node set is the Cartesian product of the one-dimensional node sets; the
displayed finite sum is its value on any function defined on that node set.
hypotheses: Step 3.1 uses the exact tensor product formula, so each tensor weight is a product of coordinate weights; dimensions are two and all factors are positive.
